Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-polish-long-0051", "row_sha256": "ddff3c11ff8e82f63ba85d75bbb585fdea27c59c10a6f5e9e923d07b32ee77f2", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
i did the screen-reader audit for the North Quay Library's new room-booking page over three mornings in april, with the work taking place in the small training room beside the public computers. the page had gone live for staff testing but was not yet linked from the library's main website. i used a windows laptop with nvda and firefox, and also checked the same booking steps on an iphone with voiceover and safari. the audit was about whether a visitor could find a room, understand the available times, and send a booking request without needing to use the mouse. i kept the checks to those tasks and noted visual issues separately when they affected what the screen reader said.

before starting, i recorded the browser versions, screen-reader settings, and the page's test address in my notebook. the laptop was set to 150 percent zoom, while the phone text size remained at its usual setting. i used a library account created for testing, rather than a real visitor's account, and entered a made-up contact address in the request form. no booking was submitted to the library's live calendar. the test page showed rooms on the first and second floors, with capacity, equipment, and opening hours listed for each. i checked one room with a wheelchair-accessible route and one room that was described as having a fixed presentation display, because those details could affect a visitor's choice.

on the first morning, i started from the page heading and moved through the room list using the laptop keyboard. the heading was announced clearly, but the room names and their details were presented in a sequence that took some work to understand. each room had a link called “More,” and the links were not distinguishable when heard together in the links list. the surrounding text did identify the rooms, but a user had to move back and forth to connect a “More” link with its room. i also found that the capacity was read after the equipment list, while the visual page placed it next to the room name. that order was not wrong, but it made quick comparison less convenient.

the times were arranged as a set of selectable options for each room. with nvda, the selected state was announced when i reached an option, and i could change it with the keyboard. however, the available choices were spoken as start times without the corresponding end time being repeated. the page showed the duration nearby, but that information was not included in the option's accessible name. i checked morning and afternoon slots on both floors, and the issue occurred in each group. the date control accepted keyboard input, though its instructions appeared after the control rather than before it. when i entered a date that had no open slots, the page gave a message that the day was unavailable, but focus stayed on the date field instead of moving to the message.

on the second morning, i repeated the main steps with voiceover on the iphone. the room details were easier to follow when swiping down the page than when using the rotor's links list, because the repeated “More” names appeared together there too. the room filters could be reached and changed, and voiceover announced whether each was selected. after changing a filter, the results updated without a page reload. the number of matching rooms changed visually, but the new count was not announced automatically. i could still reach the updated list by continuing to swipe, so the results were present; the missing announcement was most noticeable when the list became shorter and the next room moved upward on the screen.

the request form had fields for name, email, group size, and a short note about equipment needs. the labels were announced when i moved into the fields, and the required fields were identified. the email field used an appropriate input type on the phone, which brought up the email keyboard. i deliberately left the name field empty and activated the request button. the page displayed a message saying the name was required, but it was not announced by voiceover until i navigated back to the top of the form. the same message was available to nvda after i moved through the form again. the field itself did not receive a visible error outline on the phone, although the text message was shown above it.

one detail needed to be corrected in the audit notes before they were shared with the web team. the initial spreadsheet had a copied amount from an unrelated room estimate, and that number did not describe this audit or this page. the actual cost was $71.30, not $135.57. the $71.30 was the charge for the temporary mobile data used during the second morning, when the training room's guest network was unavailable. it was recorded on the library's test expense sheet under the audit date. the rejected amount, $135.57, came from an older equipment quote in another folder and was not charged for this work.

3. Items to check with the web team

i listed the repeated “More” link names, the missing announcement of the updated room count, and the placement of the unavailable-date message as items for discussion. i also recorded that the time options did not include their end times in the spoken names, even though the page displayed the duration nearby. i did not mark the keyboard selection behavior as a failure: i was able to reach and change every time option that i tested. for the room filters, i noted the distinction between the controls working and the result count not being announced. the form's required-field message was present, but a screen-reader user had to navigate to find it, so i documented that separately from whether the form blocked an incomplete request.

the notes include the exact room names and time slots used, the operating system and browser details, and the sequence of keys or swipes for each issue. i saved screenshots of the date message and the form error, along with a short audio recording of the repeated link names. the audio was made with the test account and did not contain a visitor's personal details. i put the files in the restricted audit folder and added a plain-text copy of the findings for staff who could not access the spreadsheet. on the third morning, i checked each file name against the notebook and confirmed that the mobile and laptop observations were labeled separately. the page address remained the staff test address throughout the checks, and i did not try the booking process on the public site.", "output": "I audited the North Quay Library’s new room-booking page over three mornings in April. The work took place in the small training room beside the public computers. The page was available for staff testing but was not yet linked from the library’s main website. I used a Windows laptop with NVDA and Firefox, and checked the same booking steps on an iPhone with VoiceOver and Safari. The audit focused on whether visitors could find a room, understand the available times, and send a booking request without using a mouse. I noted visual issues separately when they affected screen-reader output.

Before beginning, I recorded the browser versions, screen-reader settings, and test-page address in my notebook. The laptop was set to 150 percent zoom, while the phone’s text size remained at its usual setting. I used a library account created for testing, not a real visitor’s account, and entered a made-up contact address in the request form. I did not submit a booking to the library’s live calendar. The test page listed rooms on the first and second floors, with each room’s capacity, equipment, and opening hours. I checked one room with a wheelchair-accessible route and another described as having a fixed presentation display, since those details could affect a visitor’s choice.

On the first morning, I started at the page heading and navigated the room list with the laptop keyboard. The heading was announced clearly, but it took some effort to understand the sequence of room names and details. Each room had a link labeled “More,” and those links were indistinguishable when heard together in the links list. The surrounding text identified each room, but users had to move back and forth to connect a “More” link with its room. I also found that capacity was read after the equipment list, although the visual page placed it next to the room name. This order was not incorrect, but it made quick comparisons less convenient.

Each room’s times appeared as selectable options. With NVDA, I heard the selected state when I reached an option, and I could change it with the keyboard. However, the options were announced as start times without repeating the corresponding end times. The page displayed the duration nearby, but that information was not part of the option’s accessible name. I checked morning and afternoon slots on both floors, and the issue occurred in each group. The date control accepted keyboard input, but its instructions appeared after the control rather than before it. When I entered a date with no open slots, the page displayed a message that the day was unavailable. Focus remained on the date field instead of moving to the message.

On the second morning, I repeated the main steps with VoiceOver on the iPhone. The room details were easier to follow by swiping down the page than by using the rotor’s links list, where the repeated “More” names appeared together. I could reach and change the room filters, and VoiceOver announced whether each was selected. After a filter changed, the results updated without a page reload. The number of matching rooms changed visually, but the new count was not announced automatically. I could still reach the updated list by continuing to swipe, so the results were available. The missing announcement was most noticeable when the list became shorter and the next room moved upward on the screen.

The request form included fields for name, email, group size, and a short note about equipment needs. The labels were announced as I moved into the fields, and the required fields were identified. On the phone, the email field used an appropriate input type and opened the email keyboard. I deliberately left the name field empty and activated the request button. The page displayed a message saying that the name was required, but VoiceOver did not announce it until I navigated back to the top of the form. NVDA users could access the same message after moving through the form again. The field did not receive a visible error outline on the phone, although the text message appeared above it.

One detail needed correction in the audit notes before they were shared with the web team. The initial spreadsheet included an amount copied from an unrelated room estimate; it did not describe this audit or this page. The actual cost was $71.30, not $135.57. The $71.30 charge was for temporary mobile data used on the second morning, when the training room’s guest network was unavailable. It was recorded on the library’s test expense sheet under the audit date. The rejected amount, $135.57, came from an older equipment quote in another folder and was not charged for this work.

3. Items to check with the web team

I listed the repeated “More” link names, the missing announcement of the updated room count, and the placement of the unavailable-date message as items for discussion. I also recorded that the time options did not include their end times in their spoken names, even though the page displayed the duration nearby. I did not mark keyboard selection as a failure: I could reach and change every time option I tested. For the room filters, I distinguished between the controls working and the result count not being announced. The required-field message was present, but a screen-reader user had to navigate to find it. I documented that separately from whether the form blocked an incomplete request.

The notes include the exact room names and time slots used, the operating system and browser details, and the sequence of keys or swipes for each issue. I saved screenshots of the date message and form error, along with a short audio recording of the repeated link names. The recording used the test account and contained no visitor’s personal details. I put the files in the restricted audit folder and added a plain-text copy of the findings for staff who could not access the spreadsheet. On the third morning, I checked each file name against the notebook and confirmed that the mobile and laptop observations were labeled separately. The page address remained the staff test address throughout the checks, and I did not try the booking process on the public site."}]
